issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Heavy Makeup: heavy make-up
issues.explanation: 'Heavy make-up' is difficult to reconcile with this patient's demographics (57-year-old male) and trauma presentation unless there is specific context not provided. It stands out as the clearest demographic/item mismatch in the five target components.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the rest of the memory profile and overall severe PTSD presentation: it sits awkwardly alongside vivid but fragmented trauma memory and strong threat/appraisal activation after sexual assault. This is a within-node tension, because easy verbal access to the trauma is hard to square with marked fragmentation and severe re-experiencing-linked formulation here.

vignette:
Arthur sits with his back pressed firmly into the corner of the waiting room chair, a position he scouted and secured the moment he arrived. At fifty-seven, his work as a private tutor requires a quiet patience he no longer feels he possesses. The event, as he calls it, happened eight months ago. He had agreed to help a new client, a university student, with a paper at his apartment. When Arthur arrived, another man was there. What followed is a memory that plays in his mind not as a coherent film, but as a series of blindingly sharp, disjointed snapshots: the scratch of a wool sweater against his cheek, the terrifying strength of hands pinning his arms, the loss of his own will as his body was forced into compliance. He can see the pattern on the carpet, he can feel the pressure on his wrists, but the sequence is broken. He knows what happened, but when he tries to assemble the pieces into a story, the words evaporate, leaving only a raw, incommunicable horror.

In the weeks that followed, the world began to shrink. He had come to believe that danger was a constant, lurking just beneath the surface of everyday life. Tutoring sessions, once a source of quiet satisfaction, became ordeals of threat assessment. He started insisting on meeting students only at the public library, always arriving early to claim a seat against a solid wall, where no one could approach him from behind. He watches people constantly, scanning their hands, their eyes, their posture for any sign of aggression. He feels a particular dread when alone with his male students. A simple, friendly gesture, like a hand offered for a handshake, sends a jolt of panic through him. He recoils instinctively, a movement so sharp and sudden it often leaves the other person confused and embarrassed. Arthur feels the shame of it, but the terror is louder. He has come to see his own body as fundamentally untrustworthy, a vessel that failed to protect him and could fail again at any moment.

His life is now governed by a rigid set of rules designed to keep him safe. He avoids any situation that might provoke a strong emotion, cancelling plans with the few friends he has left if he feels the slightest bit anxious. The idea of going to an unfamiliar restaurant or shop is unthinkable; he cannot calculate the risks, the exits, the lines of sight. Physical contact is out of the question. He wears long sleeves even in the summer, a thin barrier against the possibility of an accidental brush of skin in a crowd. This profound separation from others has left him feeling utterly alone, as if he is watching the world from behind a thick pane of glass. The only reliable comfort he has is nicotine. On bad days, when a memory fragment ambushes him or a near-touch sends his heart racing, he finds himself outside, chain-smoking, the burn in his lungs a welcome distraction from the chaos in his head.

The decision to seek help came after a long-standing client, the mother of a high school student he had tutored for two years, gently told him they wouldn’t be needing his services anymore. Her son, she explained, found Arthur’s intensity and rigid rules too stressful. The loss of income was a blow, but the realization of how his fear was perceived by others was devastating. He saw in that moment the full extent of his isolation, a prison he had built for himself, brick by brick. He is here now because the loneliness has become more frightening than the potential danger of the outside world. He doesn’t know if he can ever feel safe again, if he can ever trust another person or even his own body, but the faint hope that he might one day shake a student’s hand without flinching is, for now, enough to keep him in this chair.
